issues.issue: The preamble makes Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. the Auction Agent acting "not in its individual capacity but solely as agent of WELLS FARGO BANK, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION (the 'Tmstee')" — the same entity as its own principal, and the defined term is misspelled. A court could be asked which capacity binds and whether the agency limitation has content when principal and agent are one person.

The preamble names the Company as a contracting party, but Section 5.5 confines enforcement rights to the Auction Agent, the Bond Insurer and BD. Whether the Company is a party with rights is a genuine cross-provision question.

The recital defines the four series collectively as the "Series 2004 Bonds" and then says the same instruments are "sometimes referred to together herein as the 'Series 2004 Auction Bonds'", creating two labels for one set without a rule for when each applies. The word "sometimes" leaves the boundary between the two defined terms undrawn.

Section 1.3(f) treats "Series 2004 Bonds" and "Series 2004 Auction Bonds" as distinct referents to which any reference to "Bonds" applies, which sits awkwardly with this recital's equation of the two. Reconciling the recital with 1.3(f) is a real interpretive step.

The recital says only that BD "is to perform certain duties set forth herein" without identifying them, so it adds nothing a court could measure. Its vagueness is of the kind courts ignore rather than construe.

The recital subordinates the Auction Rate to the Indenture ("except as provided therein"), while Section 2.1(b) incorporates the Auction Procedures wholesale into this agreement; a precedence question could arise. No actual inconsistency is apparent, however.

"Unless the context clearly requires otherwise" is an undefined escape from the beneficial-ownership rule, and "clearly requires" sets no test. A party wanting record-owner meaning could invoke it in any particular section.

This deeming rule treats "Series 2004 Bonds" and "Series 2004 Auction Bonds" as separate categories, whereas the second recital says the collective Series 2004 Bonds are the Series 2004 Auction Bonds. The two definitional statements do not sit comfortably together.
The warranty is given by BD to the Auction Agent only, though the Company is a signatory; Section 5.5's beneficiary limitation raises who may sue on it. The point is thin on these words alone.

Wholesale incorporation of the Indenture's Auction and Settlement Procedures gives no order of precedence, yet Section 2.3(a) sets out its own auction schedule and BMA-holiday timing that can diverge from Exhibit B of the Indenture. A court could be asked which text governs a timing conflict.

"BD agrees to handle customer orders in accordance with its respective duties under applicable securities laws and rules" imports an undefined external standard as a contractual promise, and "its respective duties" has no antecedent. What conduct breaches this sentence is genuinely open.

The clause says Broker-Dealers "may participate in Auctions for their own accounts" without saying whether they may or must place support bids, and permits the Company to bar own-account Bids while preserving Hold and Sell Orders. Whether the permission carries any duty or disclosure obligation is the classic auction-rate dispute.

The purely permissive own-account language sits against Section 2.3(b), which obliges BD to work the auction "thereby achieving the lowest possible interest rate"; a party could argue those pull in opposite directions. The tension is arguable rather than a flat contradiction.

The confidentiality undertaking is undercut by a general "except as otherwise required by law" plus three enumerated escapes, one of which ((c)) lets the Auction Agent disclose whenever non-disclosure would expose it to any "loss, liability, claim, damage or expense" without indemnity. The reach of that catch-all against the specific list is uncertain.

The schedule may be changed "to reflect then currently accepted market practices for similar auctions", and the BMA sentence applies "unless the Auction Agent is instructed otherwise" without saying by whom. Both phrases leave the trigger and the instructing party undetermined.

The BMA sentence moves the Submission Deadline to 11:30 a.m. while the table immediately below fixes it at 1:00 p.m. (11:00 a.m. daily); the "Notwithstanding the foregoing" opener is aimed at the change-of-schedule sentence, not obviously at the table. Reading the two together requires construction.

The table row is garbled in the instrument ("Auction Agent assembles information a daily Auction Period"), so the sentence stating the Auction Agent's assembly obligation does not read as written. What the row requires must be reconstructed.

The row fixes the Submission Deadline at 1:00 p.m., which the BMA-Recommendation sentence of Section 2.3(a) overrides to 11:30 a.m. on affected days. Which prevails on a shortened trading day is a genuine cross-reading.

The row is broken mid-phrase ("Auction Agent makes determinations pursuant (by 11:30 a.m. in the case of a daily to Section 203(b)"), and "as soon as practical" sets no enforceable outer limit for non-daily periods. Both the timing standard and the sentence itself are indeterminate.

"By approximately 3:00 p.m. but not later than the close of business" fixes the deadline by an approximation and an undefined "close of business". The row is also textually scrambled in the instrument.

The parenthetical "(and thereby achieving the lowest possible interest rate on the Series 2004 Auction Bonds)" states a purpose that could be read as an independent performance standard for BD, and "other relevant documents" is undefined. Whether BD promised an outcome or only the contacting effort is the live question.

A duty to achieve the lowest possible rate is hard to square with Section 2.1(d), which leaves BD free to bid, or not bid, for its own account. The two provisions can be harmonised, but the argument is available.

Orders must be in "substantially the form" of Exhibit B "or in such other form as may be reasonably acceptable to the Auction Agent", leaving conformity to an undefined reasonableness judgment. The exposure is small because the Auction Agent's acceptance settles it in practice.

Section 2.6(a) makes departures from Auction results ineffective "unless and until" notice is given under this subsection, while this subsection lets the Auction Agent decline late notices; the interaction leaves the status of a late-noticed transfer unclear. That is a specific cross-provision gap.
